tbl16_1: A three-column table listing, for sample counts N over four equal to 1 through 7, the trapezoidal approximation to two over pi times the elliptic integral E of 0.36 and its absolute error; the error falls from about two point eight times ten to the minus three down to roughly five times ten to the minus sixteen, shrinking by a factor near three with each added node and reaching machine precision by eight independent samples.
fig16_1: Semilog plot of absolute trapezoidal-rule error against the number of independent samples N over four for Poisson's ellipse integrand; the data points fall along a straight descending line that matches a dashed reference envelope of three to the power minus N, dropping about half a digit per sample until machine precision near ten to the minus sixteen is reached at N over four about eight, confirming geometric convergence.
fig16_2: Two panels. Panel a, semilog error versus N for a random degree-ten trigonometric polynomial: the error stays of order one until N exceeds ten, then collapses to machine precision and stays there, showing exactness once N is larger than the degree. Panel b, error versus frequency k for integrating cosine of k theta with N fixed at sixteen: nearly all k give machine-zero error, with isolated spikes only at k equal to sixteen and k equal to thirty-two, the integer multiples of N, illustrating that aliased modes between N over two and N still integrate exactly to zero.
tbl16_2: A three-column table mapping five integrand classes (trigonometric polynomial, finite-smoothness C-k, strip-analytic, entire, and C-infinity but non-analytic) to their Fourier-coefficient decay and the resulting trapezoidal error rate, ranging from exact through algebraic, geometric, supergeometric, and subgeometric.
fig16_3: Log-log plot of absolute trapezoidal error versus N for two periodic functions: absolute value of sine of x over two in coral falling along slope minus two, and its cube in navy falling along slope minus four. Dashed envelopes for Weideman's constants pi squared over three N squared and pi to the fourth over thirty N to the fourth track each curve, the steeper slope reflecting the cubed function's extra matching odd derivatives across the period.
fig16_4: Two panels. Panel a, semilog error versus N for one over the quantity two minus cosine x: coral numerical errors and a navy dashed closed-form curve coincide down to machine precision, the error shrinking by about zero point two seven per node. Panel b, a complex-plane diagram showing a horizontal shaded strip of analyticity bounded by lines at imaginary part plus and minus about one point three two, with the integrand's poles marked just outside the strip and the trapezoidal nodes shown as coral dots along the real axis, linking the geometric rate to the imaginary distance of the nearest pole.
fig16_5: Semilog plot of absolute trapezoidal error versus N for e to the power cosine x; the data points curve downward with an ever-steepening slope rather than a straight line, tracking a dashed Bessel-function envelope of two times the square root of two pi over N times e over two N all to the power N. This steepening is the signature of supergeometric, faster-than-geometric decay, with the error reaching nearly machine precision by N equal to fourteen.
fig16_6: Two panels showing the same subgeometric error data for the C-infinity but non-analytic function exp of cosine x minus one over cosine x plus one. Panel a plots error against N on a semilog axis: the curve bends downward but never straightens. Panel b plots the same error against N to the power two-thirds: the curve becomes nearly a straight line, confirming the rate exp of minus three-halves N to the two-thirds and demonstrating how a change of horizontal axis reveals the integrand's analytic structure.
fig16_7: Semilog plot of absolute error versus N for the real-line trapezoidal rule applied to the normalized Gaussian integral, whose true value is one; the data points descend with a steepening slope that drops below a straight dashed reference envelope e to the minus pi squared over h. The actual error falls faster than the reference because the entire Gaussian admits an unboundedly widening strip, reaching machine precision by N equal to twelve.
fig16_8: Two panels for the Fourier coefficients of one over the quantity two minus cosine x. Panel a, magnitude of each coefficient versus index k on a semilog axis: the exact closed form r to the absolute k over root three (navy) and FFT values from thirty-two samples (coral dots) overlap as a symmetric tent decaying away from k equals zero. Panel b, absolute error of each FFT coefficient versus k: near machine precision across the resolved central band and rising toward the Nyquist frequency at k equal to N over two due to aliasing, yet always far below the coefficient magnitude.
tbl16_3: A four-column summary table listing the chapter's eight computational etudes with their test function, convergence class, and a one-line highlight, spanning the geometric, algebraic, supergeometric, subgeometric, and real-line regimes plus the FFT-equals-trapezoidal-rule identity.
